findings.title: Unvalidated `sort` string accepted from the query
findings.explanation: `sort` is declared as `z.string().optional()`, so any client-supplied value passes validation. Replace it with an allowlist, e.g. `z.enum(['amount', 'created_at', 'id']).default('id')`, so that only known column names are accepted and invalid values yield a 400.

findings.title: SQL injection via ORDER BY interpolation
findings.explanation: `orderBy` is built by interpolating raw user input into the SQL string (`${sort} DESC, id DESC`) and then inserted with `ORDER BY ${orderBy}`. Parameter placeholders cannot be used for identifiers, so this bypasses parameterization completely. An attacker can inject arbitrary SQL (subqueries, boolean/time-based blind extraction, e.g. `(CASE WHEN (SELECT ...) THEN amount ELSE created_at END)`), reading data from other tenants despite the `org_id` filter. Map the validated enum value to a hardcoded column fragment through a lookup object (`const SORT_COLUMNS = { amount: 'amount', created_at: 'created_at', id: 'id' } as const`) and interpolate only the value from that map.

findings.title: Keyset pagination on `id` breaks when sorting by another column
findings.explanation: The `before` cursor still filters by `id < $2`, but the ordering is now by `amount` or `created_at` first. Rows are no longer ordered by id, so a page boundary on id will skip or repeat rows across pages. For correct pagination with a custom sort, the cursor must encode the sort value and id, and the WHERE clause must use a tuple comparison such as `(amount, id) < ($2, $3)`. Alternatively, restrict sorting to the default or switch to offset pagination for non-default sorts, and document the behavior.

findings.title: No sort direction control and ambiguous semantics
findings.explanation: The direction is hardcoded to DESC. Web UIs usually need ascending sort too (e.g. smallest amount first). Consider an `order=asc|desc` parameter (also validated by enum), and make sure the cursor comparison operator flips accordingly. NULLs in nullable columns also sort first in DESC in Postgres; consider `NULLS LAST` if relevant.

findings.title: Possible performance regression without supporting indexes
findings.explanation: Sorting by `amount` or `created_at` within an org may not use an index (the current query likely uses the primary key on id). On large tables this may cause full sorts per request. Consider composite indexes such as `(org_id, amount, id)` and `(org_id, created_at, id)` for the allowed sort columns, and check with EXPLAIN.

findings.title: Stale comment
findings.explanation: The comment says `Newest first, keyset pagination on id`, which is no longer accurate when a sort is supplied. Update it to describe the default order and the pagination behavior for custom sorts.

findings.title: No tests for the new parameter
findings.explanation: Add tests covering the default order, each allowed sort value, rejection of an invalid or malicious `sort` value (expect 400), and pagination across multiple pages with a non-default sort to verify no rows are skipped or duplicated.
